docs.title: The Lazy Reader
docs.text:
For people who will not read the manual.

This is a small, illustrated guide to the ideas inside aihc, a Haskell compiler. Each chapter has one idea, one picture, and one playground. The playground is the compiler itself. It runs in your browser.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
Chapter 1 Hello, compiler Text becomes a tree. Watch the parser work.

Chapter 2 Who is who Every name gets a color. Find out which x is which.

Chapter 3 What is what The compiler guesses the types. It guesses well.

Chapter 4 The honest language System FC, where nothing is implicit. Not written yet.

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text:
You do not need to know Haskell well. You do not need to know how a compiler works. That is the point.

Each chapter ends with a playground. Change the code on the left, and the compiler answers on the right. The compiler is aihc, compiled to WebAssembly by aihc. It needs a recent browser: Chrome, Firefox, or Safari 27.

If you want the long version, the manual has it. This guide has the short version, with pictures.

docs.title: Hello, compiler
docs.text:
A compiler is a program that reads a program. It reads text that a person wrote, and it writes a program that a machine can run. This chapter is about the first step: how text becomes a tree.

TEXT double x = x + x TREE define double + x x PROGRAM func $double local.get 0 local.get 0 i64.add end This chapter is about the first arrow. The second arrow takes the rest of the book.

docs.title: Run a program
docs.text:
Change the Haskell module on the left. Select Run to compile it and see its output on the right. Select Stop to stop the program.

module Main where

main :: IO ()
main = putStrLn "Hello, compiler!"

The module must have the name Main and a main function. You can import modules from aihc-prim and aihc-base, which includes Prelude. The browser compiles the module and runs the WASI P3 program. The first run must load the compiler tools and core libraries.

docs.title: Words first
docs.text:
To a computer, a program is one long line of characters. The letters d, o, u, b, l, e are six characters. They are not yet a word.

The first thing the compiler does is to read the characters and to group them into words. A programmer calls these words tokens. double is a token. So is =, and so is +. A space between two tokens is not a token. It only keeps them apart.

This step is small, and the compiler does it fast. The interesting part comes next.

docs.title: A tree, not a list
docs.text:
Read this sentence: the cat sleeps on the book. You did not read it as six separate words. You read the cat as one thing, on the book as another, and sleeps as the action that connects them. The words have a shape.

A program has a shape too. In double x = x + x, the + connects two things, and the = connects a name to a body. The compiler finds this shape. The result is a tree: one node at the top, and smaller pieces below it. The part of the compiler that does this is the parser.

Here is the parser of aihc. Write a little Haskell on the left, and look at the tree on the right.

double x = x + x

greeting = "hello"

Try this

  • Add a third line: big = double (double 10). The parentheses are in the text, but not in the tree.
  • Remove the = from the first line. The parser tells you where it got lost.
  • Write answer = if True then 1 else 0. An if has exactly three children. Find them.

docs.title: One question left
docs.text:
The tree has two nodes that say x. Are they the same x? The parser cannot tell. It finds the shape of the text, and nothing else.

Next chapterWho is who

docs.title: Who is who
docs.text: The parse tree is full of names. Two names can look the same and mean different things. Before the compiler can do anything with a program, it must know, for every name, where that name was defined.

docs.title: The same letter, twice
docs.text:
Look at this program.

double x = x + x

twice f x = f (f x)

There are four x in it. The first two belong to double. The other two belong to twice. They are different things that happen to share a letter. If double changed its x, twice would not notice.

The compiler must know this. So it walks through the tree, and for each name it finds the place where that name was born. A programmer calls this step name resolution. In aihc, a component called aihc-resolve does it, and it does nothing else.

docs.title: Every name gets a color
docs.text:
Here is name resolution, with colors. Each thing that was defined gets one color. Every use of that thing gets the same color. A name with a darker underline is the place where the thing was born. Hold the mouse over a name to see where it comes from.

double x = x + x

twice f x = f (f x)

four = twice double 1

Some names come from outside the program. + is one of them. The reader did not define it, and the compiler finds it in the Prelude, the library that every Haskell program gets for free. The list under the code says where each name comes from.

Try this

  • Rename the x of double to n. Only the colors of double change.
  • Write shadow x = (\x -> x) x. The inner x hides the outer one, and gets its own color.
  • Write oops = missing 1. The compiler does not find missing, and says so.

docs.title: Why this comes first
docs.text:
Name resolution looks like a small step, and it is. But everything after it depends on it. The next chapter asks what type each name has. That question only makes sense when the compiler knows which name is which. A good compiler answers the questions in order, and keeps each answer in its own place.

Next chapterWhat is what

docs.title: What is what
docs.text: A Haskell program can be written with no types at all. The compiler finds them anyway. This chapter shows how the compiler guesses the type of everything, and how its guesses are always right.

docs.title: Everything has a type
docs.text:
True is a Bool. 'a' is a Char. (True, 'a') is a pair of the two. A function that takes a Bool and gives a Char has the type Bool -> Char.

In Haskell, you can write the type of a thing above its definition. Most programmers do, because a type is a good comment that cannot go stale. But you do not have to. When you leave the type out, the compiler works it out from the code. A programmer calls this type inference. In aihc, the component aihc-tc does it.

docs.title: Watch the compiler infer
docs.text:
The playground below runs the type checker of aihc on your code. On the right, it shows the same code with the types it inferred, as signatures above each definition.

x = ()

double n = n + n

twice f a = f (f a)

pair = (True, "hello")

The signature of double says (Num a) => a -> a. Read it as: for any type a that is a number, double takes an a and gives an a. The compiler does not know whether you will use double on an Int or on a Double. So it does not decide. It gives the most general type that works.

The signature of twice has no Num in it. twice never adds anything. It only calls f two times, so f must give back the same type that it takes. That is all the compiler knows about f, and that is exactly what the signature says.

Try this

  • Write swap (a, b) = (b, a). The compiler finds the two types and swaps them.
  • Write apply f = f 1. The argument of f must be a number, so Num appears.
  • Write oops = True + 1. True is not a number. The compiler says what it could not match.

docs.title: The road ahead
docs.text:
Three chapters in, the compiler has read the text, found every name, and worked out every type. It has not changed the program at all. That changes in the next chapter. The compiler rewrites the program into a smaller, stricter language, where nothing is left implicit.
